subject: english-literature
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE unseen-poetry analysis task on {lo}, then mark my answer.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for GCSE unseen poetry simply, with an example and the most common mistake.
learningObjectives: Identifying poetic techniques and their effects
Building an analytical PEA paragraph with tentative language
Comparing an unseen poem with a studied poem
Applying the assessment objectives (AO1, AO2 and AO3)

questions.lo: Identifying poetic techniques and their effects
questions.q: 'The thunder growled across the hills' gives the thunder a human/animal quality. This is:
questions.explain: Describing thunder as if it can 'growl' gives it a living quality - personification - creating a threatening, animal-like atmosphere.

questions.lo: Identifying poetic techniques and their effects
questions.q: The repeated vowel sound in 'the low, cold stone' is an example of:
questions.explain: Assonance is the repetition of vowel sounds within words (the long 'o' in low, cold, stone), here creating a heavy, sombre sound.

questions.lo: Identifying poetic techniques and their effects
questions.q: A poem describes grief as 'a tide that never turns'. The best analytical point is that this metaphor:
options: Suggests grief is endless and cannot be escaped
questions.explain: The metaphor of an unturning tide suggests grief that is relentless and inescapable; analyse the idea the comparison implies, not just the image.

questions.lo: Identifying poetic techniques and their effects
questions.q: 'Dark, dripping, dreadful caves' uses alliteration mainly to:
options: Build an ominous, foreboding mood through the heavy 'd' sounds
questions.explain: The repeated plosive 'd' creates a heavy, ominous mood. Always connect the sound device to the atmosphere or feeling it builds.

questions.lo: Analysing form and structure
questions.q: A pair of rhyming lines together is called a:
questions.explain: A couplet is two consecutive rhyming lines; a rhyming couplet at the end of a poem often delivers a neat or emphatic conclusion.

questions.lo: Analysing form and structure
questions.q: 'Free verse' means the poem:
options: Has no regular rhyme scheme or fixed metre
questions.explain: Free verse has no set rhyme or metre, which can suggest natural speech, freedom, or a lack of order depending on the content.

questions.lo: Analysing form and structure
questions.q: A poem keeps a strict rhyme scheme until the final line, which suddenly does not rhyme. This break most likely:
options: Draws attention to the final line and unsettles the reader
questions.explain: Breaking an established pattern at the end jolts the reader and spotlights that line; disrupted form is a deliberate, meaningful choice to analyse.

questions.lo: Analysing form and structure
questions.q: A caesura is a deliberate pause within a line, often made by punctuation. Its effect is usually to:
options: Interrupt the flow and force emphasis or reflection
questions.explain: A caesura breaks the flow mid-line, forcing a pause that can add emphasis, hesitation or a moment of reflection.

questions.lo: Analysing tone, mood and voice
questions.q: The 'voice' of a poem refers to:
options: The volume you read it at
The character or persona speaking the poem
questions.explain: The voice is the speaker or persona through whom the poem is delivered, which need not be the poet themselves.

questions.lo: Analysing tone, mood and voice
questions.q: A poem mocks its subject with exaggerated praise it clearly does not mean. The tone is best described as:
questions.explain: Praise the poet clearly does not mean signals an ironic or sarcastic tone; recognising irony prevents you from misreading the poem literally.

questions.lo: Analysing tone, mood and voice
questions.q: Cold, harsh imagery and a lonely first-person voice most likely create a mood of:
questions.explain: Cold, harsh imagery with a lonely speaker builds a mood of isolation and desolation; mood is the atmosphere the reader feels.

questions.lo: Building an analytical PEA paragraph with tentative language
questions.q: In a PEA paragraph, the 'E' stands for:
questions.explain: PEA = Point, Evidence, Analysis. The Evidence is a short, well-chosen quotation that supports your point.

questions.lo: Building an analytical PEA paragraph with tentative language
questions.q: Which sentence uses the most effective tentative language?
options: The poem is definitely about death.
This proves the poet was miserable.
The imagery may hint at the speaker's hidden fear.
This clearly means one thing only.
questions.explain: 'May hint at' shows exploratory thinking. Tentative language ('may', 'perhaps', 'could') suits poems that support more than one reading.

questions.lo: Building an analytical PEA paragraph with tentative language
questions.q: Which is the best 'zoom in' analysis of a single word?
options: The adjective 'brittle' suggests the friendship could shatter at any moment.
questions.explain: Choosing one word ('brittle') and drawing out its connotations (fragility, near-breaking) is precise, high-level AO2 analysis.

questions.lo: Comparing an unseen poem with a studied poem
questions.q: In OCR's poetry component, the unseen poem is usually:
options: Compared with a poem you have studied from your cluster
Ignored in favour of the anthology
questions.explain: OCR asks you to compare the unseen poem with a taught poem from your studied cluster; using only one poem caps your marks.

questions.lo: Comparing an unseen poem with a studied poem
questions.q: When comparing the unseen poem with your studied poem, the strongest approach is to:
options: Write all about the studied poem first, then the unseen poem separately
Link the two poems on shared ideas or methods, moving between them
Compare how long each poem took to read
questions.explain: An integrated comparison that moves between both poems on shared ideas or methods is far stronger than treating each poem in isolation.

questions.lo: Comparing an unseen poem with a studied poem
questions.q: Which sentence best compares the two poems' methods?
options: Whereas the studied poem uses gentle enjambment to suggest calm, the unseen poem's abrupt caesuras convey conflict.
The studied poem is older than the unseen poem.
questions.explain: A comparative connective ('Whereas') links a specific method in each poem to its differing effect - genuine comparison of the writers' methods.

questions.lo: Applying the assessment objectives (AO1, AO2 and AO3)
questions.q: Which assessment objective rewards analysing the writer's use of language, form and structure to create meaning?
questions.explain: AO2 rewards analysis of the writer's methods and their effects, using subject terminology - central to strong poetry answers.

questions.lo: Applying the assessment objectives (AO1, AO2 and AO3)
questions.q: In OCR's poetry component, briefly linking a poem to relevant context relates to which assessment objective?
questions.explain: AO3 rewards showing an understanding of the relationships between texts and the contexts in which they were written, though it carries fewer marks here.

questions.lo: Applying the assessment objectives (AO1, AO2 and AO3)
questions.q: A student writes only about the unseen poem and never mentions the studied poem. The main problem is that they:
options: Have not compared, so cannot reach the higher levels
questions.explain: OCR's mark scheme caps responses that discuss only one poem; comparison of both poems is required to access the top levels.
